articles.title: Ukraine's drones reach Siberia again: what flies 2,500km and what it is hitting
tldr: Monitoring channels say drones hit a petrochemical plant and an Ozon warehouse in Omsk, 2,500km away; Russia confirms only a drone attack on a 'logistics hub'.
This is not new reach: Omsk's refinery was hit in July and on 8 October, reportedly by Fire Point FP-1s.
The targets are shifting from oil towards missile inputs: electronics, synthetic rubber, titanium.
body: Late on Friday the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova Plus reported strikes in Omsk, about 2,500km from the border. A fire broke out at Omsky Kauchuk, one of Russia's largest petrochemical plants, which makes synthetic rubber and a petrol additive; the channel claims it also supplies rocket fuel for Iskander missiles. An Ozon online-retail warehouse was reportedly hit as well. The regional governor, Vitaliy Khotsenko, confirmed only that "a logistics hub in Omsk was attacked by a drone". Kyiv has not claimed the strike, and the Kyiv Independent could not verify it.

Two details in the early reports need correcting. This is not a new range record: Ukraine first hit the Omsk refinery, Russia's largest, on 6 July and again on 8 October. And the Oryol strike and the closure of Moscow's airports came on 23 October, a day before Omsk; the General Staff confirmed Oryol on the 24th.

Nobody has said which drone flew to Omsk this time, and Ukraine rarely does. But two types carry most of the deep campaign. The FP-1, made by the private firm Fire Point, is a launcher-fired, twin-boom kamikaze drone weighing 60–120kg and costing about $55,000, EUobserver reports. The original reaches about 1,600km. Militarnyi says FP-1s made the 8 October Omsk strike, and that an upgraded model, renamed FP-6 and in service since July, has a wider wing that doubles as a fuel tank; Fire Point's designer, Denys Shtilerman, claims up to 3,400km.

The state-built An-196 Liutyi, from Antonov and Ukroboronprom, takes off from a runway like a light aircraft, weighs up to 300kg and carries a 50–75kg warhead. At about $200,000 it costs roughly four times an FP-1. EUobserver says it navigates by matching camera images against stored pictures of the target, reportedly without Starlink. Zelensky said an upgraded version, which Militarnyi credits with up to 2,500km, hit the Ukhta refinery in Komi, about 1,700km away, on 9 October. The jet-powered Bars is faster but, at a reported 1,000km, shorter-legged.

What is being hit matters as much as how far. Through the summer the campaign went after refineries: EUobserver reports that Russia extended its petrol export ban to 31 January 2027 amid its worst fuel crisis since the Soviet collapse. This week's targets lean towards weapons inputs. On 23 October drones hit the Proton-Electrotex electronics plant in Oryol, which reportedly supplies parts for Iskander-M missiles and Pantsir air defences; the General Staff said the strike "complicates the production of components" for cruise and ballistic missiles. On the 24th it reported hits on the Tolyattikauchuk synthetic-rubber plant, saying such rubbers go into solid rocket fuel, and on an aircraft at Yeysk. On Sunday monitoring channels claimed a strike on the Avisma titanium-sponge plant in Berezniki, more than 1,400km away; Perm's governor said 11 drones were downed and an industrial site slightly damaged, with five workers hurt.

The Moscow raid on 23 October showed the side-effects. Flights were suspended at Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo and Zhukovsky; Sheremetyevo had 85 cancellations and 229 delays, and the mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, said 17 drones were shot down. Zelensky says Ukraine does not threaten civil aviation, but that airlines and insurers should price drone risk in Russian airspace into their decisions.

The logic, as the analyst Visingr put it to EUobserver, is that "Russia simply cannot cover 100 percent of its territory with air-defence systems". The caution: many of these hits rest on monitoring channels, Russian governors routinely report most drones downed and damage "minor", and the true effect on missile output is not yet visible.

articles.title: Industry tells MPs the Defence Investment Plan is 'not investable as it stands'
tldr: Make UK's Stephen Phipson told the Defence Committee firms will not build factories on the plan as written: it has themes but no contracts or programme detail.
ADS's Kevin Craven said the plan is detailed only for four years, to 2029, and sketches roughly 50–55% of ten-year spending.
Spending ramped up late in the period would hit a bottleneck, he warned, because a new production line takes two to four years to build.
body: The Defence Investment Plan was supposed to give industry the confidence to expand. Its biggest trade bodies have now told MPs it does not. Giving evidence to the Commons Defence Committee, Make UK chief executive Stephen Phipson said: "This is not investable as it stands at the moment." The direction of travel was welcome, he said, but the contracts, programmes and procurement detail that firms need before building new capacity were missing. The UK Defence Journal reported the session on Saturday.

The plan was published on 30 June and sets out £298bn of investment over the next four years, according to ADS, the aerospace and defence trade body. ADS welcomed it at the time and said the real test would be turning it into contracts. On the evidence given to MPs, that test has not yet been passed.

ADS chief executive Kevin Craven explained the gap. The old defence equipment plan laid out a detailed pipeline of purchases over ten years. The new plan concentrates on the first four, up to 2029, and in rough terms accounts for about 50% to 55% of total spending over the decade. Some money has been brought forward to improve readiness, he said, but there is not enough detail to give firms certainty. "Intent is not the same as a commitment that is suitable for investors in defence," he told the committee.

Craven's sharper warning was about timing. Industrial capacity cannot be switched on overnight: building a new production line from scratch takes two to four years, depending on what is involved. If spending is pushed towards the end of the period, firms will all compete for the same skills, money and materials at once, creating a bottleneck just when the armed forces need the kit.

Liberal Democrat MP Ian Roome asked how damaging it would be if the next spending review failed to provide a funded path towards defence spending of 3% of national income, and whether industry would invest on the current plan regardless. Phipson's answer was no: firms will invest only once the shape of the programme is certain. ADS has called for a "clear and deliverable trajectory" to 3% of GDP by 2030 and 3.5% by 2035.

Julian David of techUK added that delay itself costs the country money, because inflation and shortages of electronic components push up prices the longer orders are held back. Arnab Dutt of the Federation of Small Businesses also gave evidence.

The counter-argument is that the plan is not empty: ADS itself said in June that its clarity would help industry, and some spending has been brought forward for readiness. But for manufacturers being asked to commit capital, the message from the witness table was consistent: a theme is not an order book.
articles.why_it_matters: Any UK manufacturer weighing defence work faces the same problem the trade bodies describe: without named programmes and contract timing, it is hard to justify new capacity.

articles.title: What is known about the UK-German 2,000km Deep Precision Strike missile
tldr: Defence minister Luke Pollard hosted Germany's armaments state secretary Jens Plötner at Lancaster House on 15 October to review Deep Precision Strike.
The programme is studying two missiles, a stealthy cruise missile and a hypersonic glide vehicle, with a range beyond 2,000km and service entry in the 2030s.
Hard details are scarce: no cost, no performance figures and no named prime contractor have been published.
body: Britain and Germany are developing a missile that could hit targets more than 2,000km away. On 15 October Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, hosted Jens Plötner, Germany's State Secretary for Armament and Innovation, at Lancaster House to review the programme, called Deep Precision Strike, and the two countries' wider defence-industrial work. Below is what is on the public record, and what is not.

The meeting. The talks took place under the UK–Germany Ministerial Group on Equipment and Capability Cooperation. Also present were Rupert Pearce, Britain's National Armaments Director, and his German counterpart, Vice Admiral Carsten Stawitzki. A panel at the German Embassy included Philipp Kerth of Hypersonica and Katherine Williams of Rolls-Royce. Pollard called Germany "one of our closest and most valued defence partners", the UK Defence Journal reported.

The weapon. Range is the one hard figure: more than 2,000km, according to the Ministry of Defence. Service entry is expected in the 2030s. In a written answer to Conservative MP Stuart Anderson in August, Pollard said: "The programme includes Stealthy Cruise and Hypersonic Glide Vehicle missile solutions." The first relies on low detectability and powered flight; the second is launched, travels at hypersonic speed and manoeuvres towards its target. The work starts with ground-launched missiles, with air- and sea-launched versions to be explored later.

The paperwork. The programme was promised in the Trinity House Agreement of October 2024, which covers air, land, maritime, cyber and space cooperation and now sits under the Kensington Treaty signed in July 2025. A memorandum of understanding signed in March 2026 let British and German teams align their military requirements and start work with industry. The MoD says the programme is open to other countries.

Where it stands. According to Pollard's August answer, joint teams are delivering technical work already contracted with industry and preparing follow-on contracts. He reported "positive alignment" on key programme parameters. UK funding is "outlined under the Defence Investment Plan".

What is missing. No programme cost has been published. Neither government has released performance figures beyond range, propulsion details or launch platforms, and the MoD names no companies as contractors. The appearance of Rolls-Royce and Hypersonica on the embassy panel shows who is in the conversation, not who has the work. Given industry's complaint this week that the Defence Investment Plan lacks programme-level detail, a missile with a range but no published budget is a fair example of the problem.

The wider relationship. Germany is already operating from Britain: German P-8 Poseidon patrol aircraft crews have flown from Lossiemouth, and Rheinmetall has expanded in the UK, including a gun barrel factory at Telford announced under Trinity House. During the Prime Minister's visit to Berlin on 8 October the two countries agreed to deepen space cooperation and to set up a Counter-Hybrid Partnership against grey-zone threats.

articles.title: The MoD's new 'front door' for small firms, and what a defence start-up should know
tldr: The MoD will publish a single guide to its procurement entry points for small and medium-sized firms by the end of 2026.
It wants to lift direct SME spending from £1.24bn in 2024/25 to £2bn in 2027/28, part of a £2.5bn rise in total SME spend by summer 2028.
The routes in already exist: the Defence Sourcing Portal, Commercial X for contracts up to £50m, UK Defence Innovation and the Office for Small Business Growth.
body: The Ministry of Defence will publish a simple "front door" listing its procurement entry points for small and medium-sized firms by the end of this year. Defence minister Luke Pollard made the promise in answers to Conservative MP Matt Vickers, the UK Defence Journal reported on Friday. Below is the practical detail a would-be founder needs.

The money. Defence spends about £5bn a year with SMEs, according to the MoD's SME Action Plan published in July. Only around a quarter goes on direct contracts; the rest flows through prime contractors' supply chains. The target is an extra £2.5bn a year by summer 2028, a 50% rise. Direct SME spend was £1.24bn in 2024/25, out of £31.6bn of total procurement. The targets are £1.48bn in 2026/27 and £2bn in 2027/28, with indirect spend rising from £4.5bn to £5.5bn. About 12,000 SMEs already sit in defence supply chains.
Who counts. Under the Procurement Act 2023, an SME has fewer than 250 staff and either turnover of £44m or less or a balance sheet of £38m or less.

Where to start. Pollard said the MoD always encourages SMEs to join the Defence Sourcing Portal "in the first instance". Opportunities going to open competition are flagged as pipeline notices on the Find a Tender platform. The Defence Office for Small Business Growth, set up in January, offers a website, a contact centre and an anonymous helpline. The SME Commercial Pathway is now public.

Faster routes. Commercial X handles contracts of up to £50m and under two years, and runs the Neutral Vendor Framework for Innovation, a Dynamic Marketplace and the Defence Unicorn Fund. UK Defence Innovation holds what the plan calls a "significant budget" for SME investment and runs regional defence and security clusters. Dstl has a Co-Creation Portal and a sister company, Ploughshare, which licenses its technology.

Help on offer. A three-month accelerator pilot run by the High Value Manufacturing Catapult and Make UK Defence is taking 20 SMEs. A separate scheme, Vanguard, run by Make UK Defence and AWS, gives five businesses a shared budget of over £750,000 in its first phase. The Defence Exports Unit offers free export support. Supplier events run through the Defence Sourcing Portal and trade shows such as DSEI and DPRTE.

The rules on bidding. Pollard said the law and MoD policy require experience, financial-standing and accreditation demands to be proportionate to each contract. The action plan promises less unnecessary bidding paperwork and a published share of direct SME spend at least once a year.

The timetable. The action plan sets dated steps: a guide to entry points and portals from the second quarter, which is the "front door" Pollard has now promised by December; a pledge for strategic partners and prime contractors on working with small suppliers; a review of social value, offsets, consortium bids and open frameworks from the third quarter; and digital self-help tools with out-of-hours support by the fourth. Small firms also get a voice through the Defence Industrial Joint Council.

Other pots. The plan points to a £250m Defence Growth Deals programme and a £182m skills package under the Defence Industrial Strategy. The MoD also promises to engage lenders ahead of a Defence Finance and Investment Strategy and to make clear that ESG rules do not hinder defence finance.

The catch. The figures Pollard gave for Tees Valley show how hard direct work is to win. Small firms there won two direct MoD contracts worth £1.48m in 2023/24, two worth £322,000 in 2024/25 and none in 2025/26. techUK has welcomed the plan but said no activity in it has a named owner and the small business office will need far more capacity. The realistic first step for most start-ups is still a subcontract to a prime, not a direct MoD contract.

articles.title: China protests UK border searches and phone seizures of its nationals
tldr: China's embassy says several Chinese nationals, including trade delegates, were held and questioned at length at the UK border and had phones and other devices seized.
Beijing says it has lodged "stern representations"; the embassy says the officers cited the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019. No UK statement has been published.
It comes three weeks after MI5's first public alert naming a Chinese research funder as a front for Beijing's spy agency.
body: China has formally protested to Britain over the treatment of its citizens at the UK border. The facts as reported:

What happened. On Tuesday 20 October the Chinese embassy in London posted a notice on its consular WeChat account saying several Chinese nationals had been held and questioned for long periods when entering or leaving the UK. In several cases officers seized mobile phones and other personal electronic devices. Those affected included members of Chinese trade and business delegations, people visiting relatives and ordinary tourists.

What is not known. The embassy gave no number of cases, no dates, no names and no length of detention. The published accounts, including those of Chinese state media Global Times and CGTN, relay the embassy's notice. No UK government response has been published.

The legal basis. According to the embassy, British officers said they were acting under "relevant provisions" of the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019. The embassy did not say which. That Act's Schedule 3 is the power aimed at state threats: it lets officers stop, question, search and detain a person at a UK port to determine whether they are involved in "hostile activity" on behalf of a foreign state, and to retain, copy, use and destroy articles found in a search. Its use is overseen by the Investigatory Powers Commissioner, who can authorise keeping or destroying material and reports on how the power is used. Whether Schedule 3 was the provision used here has not been confirmed.

Beijing's response. China has expressed "grave concern", lodged "stern representations" with the UK and will keep urging Britain to stop what it calls arbitrary detention and questioning, CGTN reported. The embassy told citizens to protect their property and privacy and to learn UK border rules.

The backdrop. On 30 September MI5 issued its first independently published espionage alert, naming the China General Technology Research Institute as a front for China's Ministry of State Security. MI5 said more than 100 UK-based academics had worked on projects it funded in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, covert communications and steganography. Security Minister Dan Jarvis wrote to university leaders asking them to end ties; those who carry on risk prosecution under the National Security Act 2023. The embassy called the accusations fabricated, and earlier this month also rejected espionage claims by the head of MI5, Global Times reported.

The stakes. China is Britain's third-largest trading partner, and the government has been trying to improve trade ties, including approving plans this year for China's largest embassy in Europe, in London. The border row shows how hard it is to run that policy alongside a tougher stance on espionage.

At Pulmuone's tofu lines, Aizera's process AI proposes coagulant and cutting changes when quality drifts.
Plans are tested in digital twins, kept within safe ranges, and the AI loses control if anything looks unfamiliar.
body: Seoul Economic Daily reports on 21 October that a group of Korean industrial-AI firms is moving beyond defect spotting to setting process conditions themselves. Three examples stand out.

Food: Aizera works on Pulmuone's tofu lines. It merges coagulation, pressing and cutting data into one time-series database, corrects clock differences between machines and works out dwell time per stage. A quality AI watches coagulation state and weight deviation; a process AI then proposes changes to the coagulant supply ratio or cutting conditions. The report says it proposes; it does not say it acts unaided.

Steel: Innergy runs predictive control on the furnace of KG Steel's continuous galvanising line. It sets zone temperatures from the current coil and the next coil's thickness, grade and sequence, and feeds them into the live control system. Its optimiser trades quality against fuel: a hotter furnace improves sheet quality but uses more fuel.
Batteries: on an EV battery line, a MakinaRocks agent re-checks a defect call; if the part is judged good, it restarts the equipment and adjusts pressing torque.

The hard part is data plumbing. Sensors log every second, but inspection results arrive only after a batch ends, so data must be aligned for transit time between stages and for machine clocks that disagree.

Safety rules are strict. Control plans are tried in a virtual factory trained on plant data, the AI may only search within the equipment's safe range and what operators allow, it loses control authority and alerts a manager in unfamiliar situations, and the plant falls back to conventional control on failure. Innergy's chief executive, Choi Jae-sik, wants PLC and DCS interlocks kept separate from the AI and control granted in stages by process risk. Retrained models are deployed only if they beat the current one.

The backdrop: Nvidia and Siemens are pushing the same idea at Siemens' Erlangen electronics plant, which the companies say now runs about 100 AI agents; their joint industrial AI operating system aims to lift factory automation from about 30-40% today to as much as 70-80%. No yield or savings figures were given for the Korean sites.

articles.title: Industrial Next's retool-in-minutes robots: nothing to buy yet, but ideas to copy
tldr: Ex-Tesla founders say their robot stations learn new tasks by simulation and demonstration, not code, and retool in minutes.
Proof so far is phone assembly for an unnamed customer and an evaluation, not an order, from BMW.
KHD cannot buy it today; the transferable lesson is to make its own kit and service easier to set up and teach.
body: Industrial Next, a San Francisco start-up shown on TechCrunch's Startup Battlefield stage on 13 October, builds self-contained robot stations driven by its own foundation models, which link vision, task context and motion. New tasks are taught by simulation and demonstration rather than hand-written scripts, and the company says a line can be retooled "in minutes rather than weeks".

It was founded in 2021 by two former Tesla engineers: Lukas Pankau, once Tesla's lead electrical architect who later worked at Waymo, and Allen Pan, who led Tesla's autonomous factory work. Robots first practise in a high-fidelity simulator built to match real-world physics, which Pankau says gives them "an understanding of the process in general".

The claimed results are specific but unverified. Stations already help make what TechCrunch calls one of the world's most popular smartphones (the customer is not named): threading a delicate flex cable, snapping a tiny connector cap in place and peeling protective film from camera modules "at or above human speed with 100% accuracy", including on a phone model the robots had never seen. BMW's Group Technology Office has agreed to evaluate the technology. As Runtime Wire notes, that is an evaluation partnership with no named line, timetable or commercial rollout.

So, can KHD buy it? Not in any practical sense yet. Neither report gives a price, a sales model, station dimensions or a funding figure, and every application shown is small-part electronics assembly, a long way from a food factory or a small engineering workshop.

What KHD could copy is the thinking. Industrial Next's pitch is that old-style automation forces firms to simplify products to suit rigid robots, and that changeover time, not the robot, is the real cost. That applies to KHD in two ways. In its own workshop, any automation worth considering is the kind that switches quickly between products, for example between Jet System and Spinner builds, rather than a fixed cell. And for customers, KHD already sells on easy setup with no pneumatics or complex controls. Making changeover between belt types, and the training of new operators, visibly faster (short video guides, preset settings by belt type) is the same idea at KHD's scale.

The strongest counter-argument: much of this is still a start-up's claim. Until a named customer reports results or BMW places an order, treat "minutes, not weeks" as a promise rather than a benchmark.
articles.why_it_matters: Nothing to buy yet. Watch for a priced, general-purpose version; meanwhile, faster changeover between belt types and quicker operator training are a selling point KHD can build into its own systems now.

articles.title: How SLAC timed an X-ray flash lasting a few hundred attoseconds
tldr: SLAC's LCLS has measured hard X-ray pulses of about 9 keV lasting 100 to 400 attoseconds, a record for an X-ray free-electron laser.
Making the pulses was not the hard part; proving how short they were was, done with a copper foil and two detectors.
Pulses that short can catch electrons deep inside atoms, and dense plasmas, before they move or the X-rays damage them.
body: Researchers at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in California report in Nature Photonics (published 20 October; lead author Ichiro Inoue of the University of Tokyo) that the Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS) produced hard X-ray pulses of about 9 kiloelectronvolts lasting between 100 and 400 attoseconds. That is the shortest high-energy pulse yet recorded at an X-ray free-electron laser. Here is the physics, step by step.

Step one: how the machine makes X-rays. A UV laser hits a copper plate and knocks out a burst of electrons. A section of SLAC's linear accelerator drives them to very high energy, and then they pass through an undulator: thousands of magnets a few millimetres apart with alternating poles. Each magnet pushes the electrons the other way, so they wiggle, and wiggling charges radiate. The clever bit is that, as they travel, the electrons organise themselves into thin parallel sheets, so the light they emit stays in step and adds up like a laser instead of a lamp. SLAC says this makes pulses about a billion times brighter than synchrotron X-ray sources. Normal LCLS pulses last femtoseconds, thousandths of a trillionth of a second.

Step two: what the numbers mean. An attosecond is 10^-18 seconds, a thousand times shorter than a femtosecond. In 100 attoseconds light travels only about 30 nanometres. A 9 keV photon has a wavelength of roughly 0.14 nanometres, around the spacing of atoms in a solid. "Hard" X-rays, above 5 keV, get deep into material and can pin down where electrons sit at atomic scale; "soft" X-rays, below 5 keV, suit the outer electrons in chemical bonds. Agostino Marinelli's SLAC team made soft attosecond X-rays in 2019. This is the step up to hard ones.

Step three: why shortness matters. Think of a camera flash. Electrons inside atoms move on attosecond timescales, so a longer flash blurs them. Marinelli says the new pulses are "fast enough to record electronic motion frozen in time". There is a second benefit: intense X-rays damage what they hit, but a short enough pulse is over before the damage happens. Inoue says it lets researchers capture an electronic state "in its pristine state".

Step four: the hard part, proving it. No detector can time a flash this short directly, and Marinelli calls the measurement "really, really difficult". Part of the reason is basic wave physics: the shorter a pulse, the wider its spread of photon energies must be, but a broad spectrum alone does not prove a pulse is short, because a long, messy pulse can be broad too. So the team took two readings of the same shot. Part of the beam went to a detector that recorded its spectrum. The rest was focused to a spot about 150 nanometres wide on copper foil. The copper atoms, hit hard, fluoresced forwards in a burst of amplified spontaneous emission, and that light carries information about the incoming pulse's energy, shape and duration. Combining the two gave the length. SLAC's account does not set out the analysis in detail; that is in the paper. Marinelli says it is the first diagnostic to show the pulses are only a few hundred attoseconds long.

What it is for: Oxford plasma physicist Sam Vinko says the pulses let his group measure core-excited states in dense plasma, like those in stars and fusion experiments, "before they had time to evolve". Tais Gorkhover of the University of Hamburg hopes they will help "truly disentangle nuclear and electronic dynamics" in imaging, and speculates they might one day help control how matter interacts with light.

The fair caveat: the press accounts give no uncertainty figures or pulse energies, and the range of 100 to 400 attoseconds is wide. The value is less a single number than a measurement method that now works at hard X-ray energies.

The one-day programme covers food economics, resilience, EU realignment, allergens, fraud and GLP-1s, with speakers from Mondelez, Compleat Food Group and Baker&Baker. Handtmann is networking partner. A possible place to meet UK factory technical and operations staff.

sources.title: Food Manufacture 360 to debut in Birmingham - February 2027

briefs.title: French ready-meal maker Fleury Michon buys Allplants
briefs.summary: Fleury Michon, the French charcuterie, ready-meal and surimi maker founded in 1905, has bought plant-based ready-meal brand Allplants from Ella and Matt Mills, who rescued it from administration in early 2025. Terms were not disclosed. The Mills family says it will now focus on soup manufacturing, distribution and media. Another sign of continental groups buying into UK chilled and frozen food.

sources.title: Allplants sold to French food manufacturer

briefs.title: Ousted Starmer-era ministers press Healey for a pro-business Budget
briefs.summary: About 30 Labour backbenchers, including former cabinet ministers Steve Reed, Darren Jones and Peter Kyle, met on Tuesday to urge Healey to cut business costs and stick to his plan not to raise capital gains tax. A Public First poll found only 26% think Labour is good for business. Healey told the Times he would back "bloody-minded" entrepreneurs.

sources.title: Former Starmerite Ministers Push For Pro-Business Budget Policies

briefs.title: Burnham asks ministers to look at scrapping gas standing charges
briefs.summary: At PMQs on 21 October Burnham asked the Chancellor and Energy Secretary to examine removing standing charges from gas bills, which average nearly 27p a day, and report back. He linked it to approving the Jackdaw gas field, expected to lift domestic gas output by 6% at peak. No funding mechanism or start date has been given; the Greens said Labour had abandoned climate credibility.

sources.title: PM Says Government Plans To Remove Standing Charges From Energy Bills

briefs.title: No 10 holds homelessness summit as pressure builds to unfreeze housing allowance
briefs.summary: Downing Street hosts a homelessness summit with MPs and charities on Monday, two days before the Budget. Burnham has pledged to end rough sleeping and put £442m towards a bed for every rough sleeper by Christmas, but councils say the Local Housing Allowance freeze is pushing people into homelessness, and there is concern it will not be uprated on Wednesday.

sources.title: No 10 To Hold Pre-Budget Homelessness Summit

briefs.title: Burnham's electoral reform push meets resistance inside his own cabinet
briefs.summary: Burnham has set up a national commission on electoral reform and promised a manifesto commitment to change the voting system, but senior figures are sceptical: Angela Rayner has called herself a "first-past-the-post girl" and Healey campaigned against AV in 2011. Around 100 Labour MPs backed the commission; More in Common warns PR could make Restore Britain a kingmaker.

sources.title: Burnham Faces Labour MP Resistance On Electoral Reform

briefs.title: Melania Trump brokers a local ceasefire to evacuate occupied Oleshky
briefs.summary: Russia and Ukraine have agreed a localised ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, mediated by Melania Trump, starting at 03:00 Kyiv time on 27 October. It is meant to let aid in and civilians leave a city cut off for months. Ukraine's ombudsman called it "extremely difficult to implement", and the roads are reported to be mined.

sources.title: Ukraine confirms Oleshky ceasefire mediated by Melania Trump between Russia, Ukraine

briefs.title: Kremlin says three-way talks with Ukraine and the US can resume after 4 November
briefs.summary: Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said on Sunday that Moscow is ready to resume trilateral talks after Russia's National Unity Day on 4 November, calling the first meeting a "trial run" and saying a deal "still needs work". Zelensky expects a round in the first half of November, possibly in Abu Dhabi. Moscow still demands the rest of Donbas.

sources.title: Moscow ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine, US after Nov. 4, Kremlin aide says

briefs.title: Seized Metro Russia gives 1 billion roubles to a war fund without Metro AG's approval
briefs.summary: Metro AG says its Russian arm, placed under Kremlin control by a Putin decree on 28 September, donated 1 billion roubles (about €11m) to a front-line equipment fund without its consent. Other seized Western firms, including Can-Pack, AkzoNobel and Rockwool, have made similar donations this year, a warning for any company still holding Russian assets.

sources.title: Kremlin-seized German company Metro AG transfers 1 billion rubles to Russian military without approval

briefs.title: Russia hits four Epicentr hypermarkets in under 24 hours
briefs.summary: Russian strikes hit four hypermarkets of Epicentr, one of Ukraine's largest retail chains, in Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Vinnytsia and Poltava on 24–25 October, injuring a woman in Poltava. The company called it the "total destruction of the network"; five of its sites had already been hit in the previous 48 hours, and by August ten of its centres had been destroyed.

sources.title: In less than 24 hours, Russia hits 4 hypermarkets belonging to one of Ukraine's largest retail chains

briefs.title: NATO's Neptune Strike runs three European carrier groups with no US carrier taking part
briefs.summary: NATO's final Neptune Strike exercise of 2026 runs from 16 October to 5 November with 17 nations, more than 20 warships and 40 aircraft, led by HMS Prince of Wales in the North Atlantic and Arctic, Italy's Cavour and Turkey's Anadolu in the Mediterranean. No US carrier group is taking part, which The Aviationist links to the US-Iran conflict.

sources.title: Three Maritime Strike Groups Spearhead NATO's Neptune Strike 26-4

briefs.title: Armed forces minister tells MPs Russia is running a sabotage campaign across Europe
briefs.summary: Armed Forces Minister Louise Sandher-Jones told Parliament that Russia is conducting "a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe" and that Britain works with the US to deter it. In a separate answer she said the UK "stands ready to defend every inch of Allied territory", citing its pledge to reach NATO's 3.5% of GDP target by 2035.

sources.title: Russia running sabotage campaign across Europe

briefs.title: Taiwan to make unlicensed AI chip and server exports to China a crime
briefs.summary: Taiwan's economics minister Kung Ming-hsin says advanced chips and AI servers will be added to the export control list, so unauthorised shipments to China could bring criminal charges under the Foreign Trade Act. The move is part of Taiwan's trade commitments to the US. No start date has been set; an August case over 130 servers had to rely on forgery and breach-of-trust charges.

sources.title: Taiwan to impose strict controls on AI chip exports to China

briefs.title: German president Steinmeier makes a five-day state visit to China from Tuesday
briefs.summary: China's foreign ministry says German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier will make a state visit from 27 to 31 October at Xi Jinping's invitation, meeting Xi, Premier Li Qiang and Zhao Leji in Beijing and Anhui province. It comes as the EU moves to cap Chinese imports, and Beijing says it hopes the trip will "cement mutual trust".

sources.outlet: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the PRC
sources.title: Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning's Regular Press Conference on October 23, 2026

briefs.title: Anthropic launches Claude Duet, a background agent for small businesses
briefs.summary: Anthropic's Claude Duet app, in research preview for Pro and Max subscribers via a waitlist, is aimed at professionals and small firms. It builds daily briefings and dashboards, runs tasks in the background on its own virtual machine and asks for approval on sensitive steps such as payments. It cannot trade securities or move money between accounts. Meta and OpenAI have rival small-business agents.

sources.title: Claude Duet app is Anthropic's bet on agents

briefs.title: Anthropic and London's Hg reportedly set up an AI consultancy
briefs.summary: Anthropic is setting up an AI consultancy with London private equity firm Hg, according to the Financial Times as reported by City AM. It is expected to launch by the end of 2026 in London and Berlin, serving B2B software companies and white-collar groups. Accenture's shares fell more than 4% on the report. Hg declined to comment.

sources.title: Anthropic partners with British private equity firm to launch consultancy arm

briefs.title: Quantum interference traps electrons inside a metal for the first time
briefs.summary: Columbia University researchers report in Science that electron waves in the layered metal Pd5AlI2 become trapped near atomic defects, a 'bound state in the continuum' previously seen only with light. Competing hopping paths for electrons cancel through destructive interference. The team says such states could aid quantum sensing and computing, and plans to place defects deliberately to tune them.

sources.title: Quantum interference traps electron waves in metal for first time
